title: The naive framing: "just add more tools?"
text: A newcomer might think a slow agent needs more tools, more context, more instructions. It's the opposite. Why does cutting a 402-line prompt make agents five times faster? You built an agent that works, but it's

title: The wrong guess: add more
text: Slow, and every call costs more than it should. The natural fix is to add more, more tools, more context, more instructions packed into the system prompt so it never misses a case. Hold on to one case, a 402-line prompt,

title: The anchor: 402 lines, 12 tools, low-stock sweep
text: 12 tools, one task, a daily low stock sweep. It took 102 tool calls and 488 seconds. But every one of those 402 lines gets

title: Breaking the wrong guess
text: Read on every call, and all 12 tools get considered even when only one applies. More isn't the problem, carrying all of it always is.

title: Three levers: tools, skills, subagents
text: Three levers trade cost for control. Tools, stateless calls ask, get an answer, decide next. Skills, instructions loaded only when needed. Sub-agents, a separate context window for a task that needs full autonomy. So, the 402-line prompt splits. The core shrinks to 15 lines, just the role, the decision logic, the output format. Five skill modules, reorder policy, forecasting, notifications, vendor lookup, audit logging, load only when a task needs them.

title: Complexity hides behind the interface
text: Here's what a skill call looks like. The core issues one instruction, run the forecasting skill. On the other side of that line, the skill loads its own 200-line sub-prompt, runs its own reasoning, and returns one result. The core never touches those lines, complexity hides behind the interface.

title: The one flag
text: One flag, these numbers five times faster, 100 seconds, are one team's measurement on one workflow. How much you gain depends on how cleanly your own task splits into bounded pieces. Back to

title: The anchor returns, decomposed
text: The sweep, same 402-line case now decomposed. The same task that took 102 tool calls and 488 seconds now runs as three scripts in about 100 seconds. Same correctness, about five times faster.

title: Both directions
text: This works when the pieces are genuinely separable. A lookup, a policy check, a template, each bounded enough to hand to a tool or a skill on its own. It flips when the task is one continuous judgment call. Splitting that just adds a boundary to cross, and the back-and-forth can cost more than the single big prompt ever did. Faster agents don't know less. They load

title: Carry-out
text: Only the knowledge each task actually needs, exactly when it needs it.

title: Your turn
text: Your turn. Here's the prompt. Read it with me. Here's my agent system prompt. Find the lines that are decision logic versus the lines that are domain knowledge. Split the knowledge into skills the agent loads on demand, and estimate the token and latency difference. Run it on your own agent and find your split. Liam Infrabear.
